At the evening aarti in the village temple, Lokesh, two, sat on his grandmother Madhuri's lap. The priest circled the lamp; the bells rang; smoke from the incense curled up.

Lokesh went completely still. His mouth fell open. He reached one hand towards the flame.

Madhuri held his hand gently back and let him watch. When the bells stopped, she guided his palms over the lamp's warmth, and he touched his eyes like everyone else.

qa.q: What did Lokesh reach towards?
qa.a: Lokesh reached towards the flame.

qa.q: What does Lokesh going completely still with his mouth open suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Lokesh felt wonder and awe at the lamp, bells and incense.

qa.q: How did Madhuri let Lokesh take part safely?
qa.a: She let him watch, gently kept his hand from the flame, and guided his palms over the warmth so he could join in.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel watching Lokesh at the aarti?
qa.a: Madhuri likely feels tender and happy to share the ritual with him.

grounding: Shows a toddler held in wonder by a temple aarti, with a grandmother letting him watch and take part gently.

passage:
On Sunday in the church in Accra, Kwame carried Elif, two, into the cool hall. The choir began to sing; candles flickered at the front.

Elif stopped wriggling. She stared at the flames, then at the singers, her eyes wide.

Kwame whispered, "Beautiful, isn't it?" and swayed gently with the music.

When everyone stood, Elif clapped softly, copying the lady beside them. Kwame smiled and let her.

qa.q: What flickered at the front of the church?
qa.a: Candles flickered at the front.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling as she stared at the flames and singers?
qa.a: Elif felt wonder and fascination, calmed by the music and candlelight.

qa.q: How did Kwame help Elif experience the service?
qa.a: Kwame let her watch quietly, shared the moment in a whisper and allowed her to join gently by clapping.

qa.q: How might the lady beside them feel seeing Elif copy her?
qa.a: The lady might feel amused and warm, glad the toddler is joining in.

grounding: Shows a toddler held in wonder by church candles and singing, with a parent letting her watch and join gently.

passage:
Every night in Mexico City, Rosa, two, climbed onto Abuela Esther's lap for the bedtime prayer.

Esther held Rosa's small hands together inside hers and whispered the words slowly. Rosa said the last word with her, "Amén," and giggled.

Then Esther kissed her forehead. "Good night, mi amor." Rosa snuggled into her shoulder, eyes closing.

qa.q: What word did Rosa say with Esther?
qa.a: Rosa said "Amén" with Esther.

qa.q: What does Rosa snuggling into Esther's shoulder suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Rosa felt loved, safe and close to her grandmother.

qa.q: Why does this bedtime ritual matter for Rosa?
qa.a: Shared warmly each night, it makes her feel part of the family and becomes a safe memory, not an obligation.

qa.q: How might Esther feel holding Rosa's hands during the prayer?
qa.a: Esther likely feels tender and joyful, passing on something precious.

grounding: Shows a toddler feeling loved and part of the family while praying on her grandmother's lap at bedtime.

passage:
Mother's note, Tuesday.

Vandana, two, had a fever all day and wouldn't be put down. Every time I tried, she wailed.

So I held her, gave her small sips of water and sang quietly. Naveen took over when my arms ached.

By evening the fever was still there and she was very sleepy, so we called the doctor, who asked us to bring her in. We did not scold her clinginess.

qa.q: Who took over holding Vandana when the mother's arms ached?
qa.a: Naveen took over.

qa.q: Why did Vandana wail every time she was put down?
qa.a: Vandana felt ill and scared, and needed the comfort and safety of being held.

qa.q: Which choices did the parents make that were right?
qa.a: They held and comforted her, gave water and rest, spoke calmly, didn't scold her clinginess, and called the doctor when she stayed feverish and very sleepy.

qa.q: How might Naveen be feeling while taking his turn?
qa.a: Naveen is probably worried about Vandana and wanting to help and comfort her.

grounding: Shows a feverish toddler who won't be put down, comforted with holding and water, with the doctor called when signs are worrying.

passage:
In their village house, Chetan, two, had a hot forehead and whimpered whenever his father Deepak put him on the mat.

Deepak picked him up and walked slowly around the courtyard, humming. He gave Chetan sips of water and stayed close.

Grandmother said, "Don't spoil him."

"He's sick. He needs me," Deepak said.

When the fever kept going next morning, they went to the health centre.

qa.q: Where did Deepak walk with Chetan?
qa.a: Deepak walked around the courtyard.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he whimpered on the mat?
qa.a: Chetan felt unwell and scared, wanting to be held.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that was right?
qa.a: He held and calmed Chetan, gave water, didn't treat clinginess as spoiling, and took him to the health centre when the fever kept going.

qa.q: How does Grandmother see Deepak holding Chetan?
qa.a: Grandmother sees it as spoiling, while Deepak sees it as comfort Chetan needs when sick.

grounding: Shows a sick toddler who wants to be held, comforted with holding and water, with a doctor visit when the fever keeps going.

passage:
At the clinic in Hanoi, Mei, two, saw the nurse's white coat and screamed. She kicked and clung to her father Tuan.

Tuan held her close on his lap. "It'll be a small pinch, then it's done. I'm right here."

Mei cried through the injection. Tuan kept holding her.

Afterwards he said, "You were brave. All done." Mei hiccupped and held her sticker.

qa.q: What did Mei hold after the injection?
qa.a: Mei held her sticker.

qa.q: Why did Mei scream and kick?
qa.a: Mei felt frightened by the white coat and strange room.

qa.q: How did Tuan help Mei through the injection?
qa.a: He stayed close, held her, told her the truth simply, a small pinch, and comforted her afterwards.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Tuan's approach?
qa.a: The nurse would probably appreciate that he was honest and calm, making it easier for Mei.

grounding: Shows a toddler frightened at the clinic, with a parent who holds her close and tells the truth simply.

Monday. Aditi's aunt told Charu, two, "If you're naughty, the doctor will give you an injection!" Aditi said firmly, "No, Masi. Doctors help."

Thursday. At the clinic, Charu cried and hid in Aditi's lap. "A small pinch, then done," Aditi said, holding her tight.

Two weeks later. Charu gave her teddy a pretend injection. "Small pinch," she told it, patting its arm.

qa.q: What did Charu give her teddy two weeks later?
qa.a: Charu gave her teddy a pretend injection.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she hid in Aditi's lap?
qa.a: Charu felt scared of the clinic and the injection.

qa.q: Why did Aditi stop her aunt's threat?
qa.a: Using the doctor as a punishment would make Charu more afraid; Aditi wanted her to see doctors as helpers.

qa.q: How might Aditi's aunt see the moment when Aditi corrected her?
qa.a: The aunt might feel surprised or a little embarrassed, having meant it as a joke.

grounding: Shows a toddler's fear of the doctor, with a parent who refuses threats, stays close and tells the truth simply.

passage:
Daycare note, Friday.

Uma, two, tripped in the yard and scraped her knee. At pickup she showed her mother, Devika, lip wobbling.

Devika knelt. "Ouch! That hurt, didn't it?" She kissed the scrape gently and hugged her.

Uma nodded, then said, "Better," and walked to the gate holding her mother's hand.

qa.q: What did Uma scrape in the yard?
qa.a: Uma scraped her knee.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when her lip wobbled?
qa.a: Uma felt hurt and upset, wanting her pain to be noticed.

qa.q: Why is Devika's response important?
qa.a: By acknowledging the hurt calmly with a kiss and hug, rather than saying it was nothing, Devika teaches Uma trust and later resilience.

qa.q: How might the note-writer see Devika's response?
qa.a: The note-writer seems to see it as a good example, recording how quickly Uma felt better.

grounding: Shows a toddler whose pain is acknowledged with a kiss and hug, teaching her it matters.

passage:
In the village lane, Trisha, two, fell and grazed her palm on the stones. She howled.

Her mother, Indu, ran over. "Oh, my baby. That really hurt." She blew on the graze, kissed it and held Trisha close.

A neighbour said, "It's nothing, don't cry!"

Indu kept rocking. "It hurt her." Soon Trisha stopped crying and went back to chasing the hens.

qa.q: What did Trisha graze on the stones?
qa.a: Trisha grazed her palm.

qa.q: Why did Trisha stop crying soon after Indu held her?
qa.a: Trisha felt comforted and safe, because her pain was taken seriously.

qa.q: How was Indu's response different from the neighbour's, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Indu acknowledged the hurt calmly, while the neighbour said it was nothing; acknowledging it teaches trust.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Trisha's fall?
qa.a: The neighbour sees it as a small thing that doesn't need tears.

grounding: Shows a toddler comforted by a kiss and hug that acknowledge her pain, rather than being told it is nothing.

passage:
Nanny's note, Sunday.

Sudha's parents started arguing loudly in the kitchen. Sudha, two, froze, covered her ears and began crying.

I picked her up. Lokesh saw her and lowered his voice. "Not in front of her," he said, and they went out to the balcony to talk.

Afterwards Lokesh knelt by Sudha. "Papa and Mama were loud. You're safe." She clung to him, then calmed.

qa.q: Where did Sudha's parents go to talk?
qa.a: They went out to the balcony.

qa.q: Why did Sudha cover her ears and cry?
qa.a: Sudha felt frightened by the shouting, sensing danger she couldn't understand.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do right once he saw Sudha?
qa.a: He lowered his voice, moved the argument away and reassured Sudha afterwards.

qa.q: How might the nanny feel during the argument?
qa.a: The nanny likely feels concerned for Sudha and focused on comforting her.

grounding: Shows a toddler frightened by parents' shouting, with adults who lower their voices, move away and reassure her.

passage:
Daycare note, Monday.

Ganga, two, arrived silent and hid under the table. When I sat nearby she said, "Papa shout. Mama cry. Ganga bad."

I held her gently. "You're not bad. You're safe here." She clung to me.

At noon I told our centre head, and we called Ganga's mother the same day. She said the shouting happens often. We gave her the family helpline number and arranged a meeting tomorrow.

— Karthik

qa.q: Where did Ganga hide when she arrived?
qa.a: Ganga hid under the table.

qa.q: What does Ganga saying "Ganga bad" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Ganga felt overwhelmed and frightened, and blamed herself for the shouting at home.

qa.q: What steps did Karthik take on the same day?
qa.a: Karthik comforted Ganga and told her she wasn't bad, informed the centre head, called her mother and shared a helpline and a meeting.

qa.q: How might Ganga's mother feel when the daycare calls?
qa.a: She may feel worried or ashamed but also supported, since help is being offered.

grounding: Shows a toddler overwhelmed by shouting at home and blaming herself, with a caregiver who comforts her and seeks help the same day.

passage:
Monday. "No sweets now," Maria said. Vishal, two, screamed and dropped to the floor. Maria shouted back, and he screamed louder.

Wednesday. "No sweets now." Vishal wailed. Maria sat nearby. "You're so cross. You wanted it." She waited.

Two weeks later. "No sweets. Want a banana?" Vishal cried a bit, then took the banana.

qa.q: What did Maria offer instead of sweets two weeks later?
qa.a: Maria offered a banana.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he dropped to the floor?
qa.a: Vishal felt a rage he had no words for, after being told no.

qa.a: She held the limit gently, named his feeling, let the storm pass and offered a safe alternative instead of shouting back.

qa.q: How might Maria feel two weeks later when Vishal takes the banana?
qa.a: Maria likely feels relieved and more confident.

grounding: Shows a toddler raging when told no, and a parent learning to hold the limit gently, name the feeling and offer an alternative.

Deepak screamed and dropped to the floor, kicking.

Jasleen crouched beside him. "You're angry. You wanted the drum." She waited while he cried.

When he quieted, she held out her keys. "Want to shake these?"

Deepak jingled the keys all the way home.

passage:
Grandmother's note, Tuesday.

Madhuri, two, wanted more biscuits. Her mother, Shreya, said, "No more, Madhuri." I said the same when she asked me.

Madhuri paused, sighed and said, "Okay," then went to her dolls.

Shreya smiled at me and said quietly to Madhuri, "Good listening." Yesterday she cried at the same no, and we didn't expect this every day.

qa.q: What did Madhuri want more of?
qa.a: Madhuri wanted more biscuits.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she sighed and said "Okay"?
qa.a: Madhuri felt a little disappointed but calm and accepting.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri accept the no this time?
qa.a: Both her mother and grandmother gave the same calm limit, and that consistency builds acceptance.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel after Madhuri moved on?
qa.a: Shreya likely feels pleased and thankful for the grandmother's support.

grounding: Shows a toddler sometimes accepting a no after calm, consistent limits from every adult, with quiet praise.

passage:
It was pouring outside, so the whole wedding crowd was packed into the hall, loud with music. Saurabh, five, and his friend Alka were playing with a toy car under a table.

Alka grabbed it. Saurabh's face went hot; his fists tightened. "MINE!" he screamed, and raised his hand.

His aunt crouched under the table, catching his hand. "Stop. Use words. Say, 'I'm angry. Give it back.'"

Saurabh glared. "I'm angry! Give it back!"

"Now a big breath," his aunt said. They breathed together.

Alka slowly handed him the car. "Your turn, then mine?"

Saurabh nodded, still frowning, but his hands had unclenched.

qa.q: Why was the wedding crowd packed into the hall?
qa.a: It was pouring outside.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when his face went hot and his fists tightened?
qa.a: Saurabh felt furious that Alka grabbed the car.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's aunt help him handle his anger?
qa.a: She stopped his hand, helped him say his anger in words, and took a breath with him.

qa.q: How might Alka feel when Saurabh uses words instead of hitting?
qa.a: Alka likely feels safer and more willing to give the car back and take turns.

grounding: Shows a young child's hot anger in a toy dispute, with an adult helping him put it into words and take a breath instead of hitting.

passage:
In the Mumbai flat, Hansa, five, was building a tower when Vandana took the red block from the top.

Hansa's cheeks flushed. She clenched her fists and yanked Vandana's hair.

Vandana cried. Hansa's mother came over, separated them and comforted Vandana. Then she knelt by Hansa. "You're angry. Say it with words: 'I'm angry. I want my block.'"

Hansa scowled. "I'm angry. I want my block."

"Good. Let's breathe." They took three slow breaths.

Vandana gave back the block. Hansa handed her a blue one. "You can have this one."

qa.q: What block did Vandana take from the tower?
qa.a: Vandana took the red block.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when her cheeks flushed and she yanked Vandana's hair?
qa.a: Hansa felt angry and frustrated that her tower was disturbed.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time instead of pulling hair?
qa.a: She could say "I'm angry, I want my block" in words and take a breath, as her mother showed.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel when Hansa gives her the blue block?
qa.a: Vandana likely feels relieved and included again after being hurt.

grounding: Shows a young child snatching and hurting in anger over a toy, and an adult helping her name the anger in words and breathe.
